title: Verification Method: Four Checks, In Order
body:
The verification method runs four checks. Check A: duplicate ids within an index — the same record id appearing twice, which breaks every lookup that assumes ids are unique. Check B: record-count mismatches — the manifest count against the actual index, line by line, record by record. Check C: broken page links — a manifest slug with no database page, which strands every link that points at it. Check D: demonstrably wrong facts — a statement provable wrong from another authoritative record in the network, not merely suspicious or unfashionable.

Order matters: A and B are mechanical and run first, because they need no judgment. C is mechanical too, but it is run separately because a missing page and a missing index are different failures with different fixes. D runs last and slowest, because it requires a second record that actually proves the first one wrong — suspicion alone never earns a fix.
demo_output:
A: duplicate ids within an index
B: manifest count vs actual index
C: broken page links (slug with no page)
D: demonstrably wrong facts, proven from another record
Order: mechanical first, judgment last.
provenance: Signature verification method; Signature databases were included in the checked sample.

title: Verification Method: Sampling Without Pretending
body:
The 2026-10-25 run sampled the network two ways. First, a systematic sample: 250 databases, every 244th entry of the 61,154-entry manifest, checked for page existence and, where a local index existed, for line-level checks. Second, a local-index subsample: the first 250 manifest entries whose local index is a local gzip file, checked with the reader each index format requires — line reader, row reader, or array parser — for duplicates, counts, and prefix agreement. Together the two samples cover 498 distinct databases, with only 2 in both.

What sampling does not do: it does not prove anything about the databases it did not touch, and this database never reports a sample result as a network result. The sample's job is to find real defects and measure their rate honestly — not to certify the whole network on a fraction of the evidence.
demo_code:
print('Systematic sample: 250 databases (every 244th of 61,154)')
print('Local-index subsample: 250 databases (first local gzip indexes)')
print('Distinct databases covered:', 498)
print('Overlap:', 2)
print('A sample measures; it never certifies the unexamined rest.')
demo_output:
Systematic sample: 250 databases (every 244th of 61,154)
Local-index subsample: 250 databases (first local gzip indexes)
Distinct databases covered: 498
Overlap: 2
A sample measures; it never certifies the unexamined rest.
provenance: Signature verification method; Signature databases were included in the checked sample.

title: Fix Rules: Proven Errors Only, Never Silent, Never Deleting
body:
Fix rules, without exception. Fix only proven errors: demonstrably wrong facts, broken links, duplicate ids, and count mismatches where the index itself proves the correct number. Flag uncertain items as "needs user call" and do not rewrite them. Never delete any record: a wrong record is corrected or annotated, not erased, because deletion destroys the evidence that a mistake was made and fixed. Never silently rewrite locked content: every fix gets a fix record in fixes.json, naming the slug, the record id, what was wrong, the evidence, and the correction.

The lane builder does not edit live data. This database delivers the fixes file; the coordinator applies fixes at merge after review. That separation is itself a safety rule: the hand that finds the defect is not the hand that changes the data, so every change passes a second pair of eyes.
demo_code:
print('FIX ONLY: proven errors (wrong facts, broken links, duplicate ids, proven count mismatches)')
print('FLAG: uncertain items -> needs user call (never rewritten)')
print('NEVER: delete a record; silently rewrite locked content')
print('EVERY FIX: a fix record (slug, id, wrong, evidence, correction)')
demo_output:
FIX ONLY: proven errors (wrong facts, broken links, duplicate ids, proven count mismatches)
FLAG: uncertain items -> needs user call (never rewritten)
NEVER: delete a record; silently rewrite locked content
EVERY FIX: a fix record (slug, id, wrong, evidence, correction)
provenance: Signature verification method; Signature databases were included in the checked sample.

title: Finding: Page Links — 250 of 250 Present
body:
Check C result: in the systematic sample of 250 databases, all 250 database pages were present. No broken page link was found in the sample. That is a genuine pass, and it is reported as a sample pass, not a network guarantee: the sample covers 250 of 61,154 slugs, and the remaining pages were not examined in this run.

What this finding does not do: it does not excuse the next run from checking pages again. Page existence is cheap to check and expensive to lose, because a single missing page breaks every record, search result, and cross-link that names its slug. The finding's practical consequence is that page checking stays in every future run, pass or not.
demo_code:
print('Systematic sample pages checked: 250')
print('Pages present: 250')
print('Broken page links found: 0')
print('Scope: sample pass, not a network guarantee.')
demo_output:

Pages present: 250
Broken page links found: 0
Scope: sample pass, not a network guarantee.
provenance: Signature verification method; Signature databases were included in the checked sample.

title: Finding: Duplicate Ids — None Found
body:
Check A result: across 255 distinct indexes checked with the reader each format requires — 237 JSONL indexes line by line, 8 row-array JSONL indexes (specs, leaks, generators, olympics, chips, apps, pixel, music) with a row reader, and 10 single-array indexes parsed as arrays — no duplicate record id was found in any index where an id field could be established. Duplicate-id checking matters because the whole network assumes an id names one record; a duplicate would silently make two records answer to one address, and every lookup, link, and merger would inherit the ambiguity.

One honest exception: in the words index, whose rows are headword-led arrays, the first field repeats 7,630 times across 1,127,335 rows. That is not reported as duplicate ids, because the first field there behaves like a headword — which legitimately repeats across senses — not like an established unique id, and calling it a duplicate finding would be a method error dressed as a result. Words is therefore counted for its record count, which matches the manifest exactly, but not for id uniqueness, which its row shape does not establish.
demo_code:
print('Distinct indexes checked with format-correct readers: 255')
print('Duplicate ids found: 0 (where an id field is established)')
print('Exception: words id-uniqueness not established by its row shape (see body)')
demo_output:
Distinct indexes checked with format-correct readers: 255
Duplicate ids found: 0 (where an id field is established)
Exception: words id-uniqueness not established by its row shape (see body)
provenance: Signature verification method; Signature databases were included in the checked sample.

title: Finding: Count Mismatches — 12 Stale Manifest Counts
body:
Check B result: of 250 indexes in the local-index subsample checked with format-correct readers, 238 matched their manifest counts exactly and 12 did not. In every mismatched case the index held more distinct, unique records than the manifest claimed — for example unit-tests: manifest 10,000 against 10,020 sequential unique ids JAH-TEST-000001 through JAH-TEST-010020 — film-public: manifest 33 against 53 sequential unique ids — and books: manifest 48,100 against 48,120 sequential unique ids JAH-BOOK-000001 through JAH-BOOK-048120. The pattern is a stale manifest stamp, not corrupted indexes: the indexes are internally clean, and the manifest simply was not restamped after the indexes grew.

Fix proposed for each of the 12: update the manifest record_count to the actual distinct-record count, as listed in fixes.json. No record is touched; only the manifest's summary number changes, to match the data it summarizes. The 12 slugs are persona-profiles, unit-tests, meta, probability-stats, code-database, world-history, graphic-design, game-design, emergency, banking, film-public, and books.

title: Finding: Fused Lines — Two Records Sharing One Line
body:
A defect the line counter nearly missed, found through the malformed-line trail: in transportation and photography, line 10,000 of each index holds two complete records fused without a newline. In transportation the fused pair is JAH-TRN-0010000 and JAH-TRN-0010001; in photography it is JAH-PHO-010000 and JAH-PHO-010001. A line-based reader counts the fused line once, so both databases' manifest counts — which equal their line counts — undercount their true records by exactly one each: transportation holds 10,100 records, photography 10,075.

Fix proposed: split each fused line into two lines at the object boundary, changing no record content, and restamp the two manifest counts up by one each. This is the run's clearest example of why a verification check must look at malformed lines instead of skipping them: the malformed line was the defect, not noise around it.
demo_code:
print('transportation line 10000: JAH-TRN-0010000 + JAH-TRN-0010001 fused')
print('photography line 10000: JAH-PHO-010000 + JAH-PHO-010001 fused')
print('True records: transportation 10100, photography 10075 (manifest counts under by 1 each)')
print('Fix: split the line at the object boundary; change no content.')
demo_output:
transportation line 10000: JAH-TRN-0010000 + JAH-TRN-0010001 fused
photography line 10000: JAH-PHO-010000 + JAH-PHO-010001 fused
True records: transportation 10100, photography 10075 (manifest counts under by 1 each)
Fix: split the line at the object boundary; change no content.

title: Finding: Prefix Disagreement — Two Manifest Prefixes Wrong
body:
Check D result, first case: two manifest id_prefix fields disagree with the actual ids in their own indexes. For public-energy-engineers-except-wind-and-solar the manifest claims prefix JAH-PEE-, but all five index records carry JAH-EEE-000001 through JAH-EEE-000005, with titles matching the slug's subject. For public-judges-magistrate-judges-and-magistrates the manifest claims JAH-PJM-, but all five records carry JAH-JMJ-000001 through JAH-JMJ-000005, again with matching titles.

Which side is wrong is decidable: the index records are internally consistent, sequentially numbered, and title-matched, while the manifest prefixes match neither the ids nor any visible abbreviation pattern. Fix proposed: correct the two manifest id_prefix fields to JAH-EEE- and JAH-JMJ- respectively. No record is renumbered; the manifest's label is corrected to match the data. Renumbering records to match a wrong label would have been the backwards fix, and it was rejected.
demo_code:
print('public-energy-engineers-except-wind-and-solar: manifest JAH-PEE- vs actual JAH-EEE-000001..5')
print('public-judges-magistrate-judges-and-magistrates: manifest JAH-PJM- vs actual JAH-JMJ-000001..5')
print('Fix: correct the manifest prefix fields; renumber nothing.')
demo_output:
public-energy-engineers-except-wind-and-solar: manifest JAH-PEE- vs actual JAH-EEE-000001..5
public-judges-magistrate-judges-and-magistrates: manifest JAH-PJM- vs actual JAH-JMJ-000001..5
Fix: correct the manifest prefix fields; renumber nothing.
provenance: Signature verification method; Signature databases were included in the checked sample.

title: Finding: Remote-Only Indexes — Unverifiable From This Clone
body:
Limitation, stated as a finding rather than buried: in the systematic sample, 243 of 250 databases carry a remote-only local_index — a jah-databases-data-1 URL rather than a local file — so their line counts could not be verified from this clone. That is not an error in those databases; it is a limit of this run's vantage point. Their pages were verified present, but their index lines were not counted, and this database does not pretend otherwise.

Flagged for user call, not fixed: whether future verification runs should fetch remote indexes for counting, or whether remote-index databases should carry a local mirror for verification. Either choice is legitimate; silently counting uncounted indexes as verified would not be. The 243 slugs are listed in the run notes held with this lane's working files, and the headline numbers in this database exclude them from every denominator they did not enter.
demo_code:
print('Systematic sample: 250 databases')
print('Remote-only index (not line-countable from this clone): 243')
print('Local index line-checked in systematic sample: 7')
print('Status: flagged for user call, NOT counted as verified.')

title: Finding: Array-Format Indexes — Resolved With Format-Correct Readers
body:
Method note, resolved rather than excused: 18 databases in the local-index subsample do not use plain JSON lines. Eight of them — specs, leaks, generators, olympics, chips, apps, pixel, music — are JSONL files whose lines are array rows, not objects; read with a row reader, all eight match their manifest counts exactly (specs 908,995, leaks 121,020, generators 137,025, olympics 38,063, chips 35,601, apps 86,194, pixel 87,000, music 108,050) with zero duplicate first-field ids. The other ten are single JSON arrays; parsed as arrays, nine match exactly with unique ids (patents 77,275, comics 18,549, news 98, aimix 38,000, robots 37,010, experiments 35,925, earth 17,300, mall 8,821, and words 1,127,335 by count), and books mismatches by 20, as recorded in the count finding.

One item remains genuinely open, and it is flagged for user call rather than smoothed over: whether the words index's repeating first field is a headword field (legitimate repeats) or an id field with true duplicates. That question needs the words builder's row schema, not another count, and until it is answered this database claims words for count only, never for id uniqueness.

print('Row-array JSONL indexes resolved: 8 (all counts match, 0 duplicate first-field ids)')
print('Single-array indexes resolved: 10 (9 match; books +20, fixed in fixes.json)')
print('Open, flagged for user call: words first-field semantics (headword vs id)')
demo_output:

title: The Fixes File: What fixes.json Contains
body:
The fixes file delivered with this pair lists 16 proposed fixes: 12 manifest count restamps, 2 fused-line splits (each with its one-count restamp noted in the same entry), and 2 manifest id_prefix corrections. Every entry names the slug, the record id or field, what was wrong, the evidence, and the correction. No entry deletes a record, rewrites record content, or touches locked content silently — and the flagged limitations above appear in this database as findings, not as fixes, because there is nothing proven to fix in them yet.

Applying the fixes is the coordinator's step, after review, not the finder's step. That is deliberate: a fix that has passed one review and one merge check is worth more than a fix applied in haste by the same run that found it, and the network's data lock-in rule exists precisely to slow down well-meaning hands.

print('   0 deletions, 0 silent rewrites, 0 record-content changes')

title: Verification Discipline: What the Next Run Must Do
body:
The next verification run has four standing tasks. One: re-run all four checks on a fresh sample, and confirm the 16 fixes were applied by re-reading the corrected manifest and indexes. Two: settle the words first-field question with the words builder's row schema, so words can be claimed for id uniqueness or flagged as a real duplicate problem. Three: decide the remote-index question — fetch or mirror — so the 243 remote-only databases stop being unverifiable from the working clone. Four: run a full page census, upgrading the supported page-coverage verdict toward proven if it passes.

Verification is not a one-time audit that ends with a clean report; it is a standing habit, run on every round, because every round adds data and every addition can carry a defect. A network that stops checking is a network that starts believing its own summaries, and this database exists to keep that from happening.
demo_code:
for t in ['Re-run 4 checks on a fresh sample; confirm the 16 fixes','Settle the words first-field question with its row schema','Decide remote-index fetching or mirroring','Run a full page census']:
    print('NEXT:', t)
